title: Fit a blood-pressure cuff on a training arm: bladder end round first, hook end over it, snug, index on the artery
instruction: Put the blood-pressure cuff on the arm: wrap the bladder end round first, then the hook end over it, press it shut, snug, with the index line over the artery mark.
context: Fitting a blood-pressure cuff is the first step of every manual or automatic reading, a routine duty of about 2.8M US workers (BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics): nursing assistants (about 1.4M; O*NET 31-1131.00: "Record vital signs, such as temperature, blood pressure, pulse, or respiration rate"), medical assistants (about 0.8M; O*NET 31-9092.00: "Interview patients to obtain medical information and measure their vital signs, weight, and height") and LPNs (about 0.63M; O*NET 29-2061.00 lists measuring and recording vital signs, including blood pressure). The AHA places the bladder's centre over the brachial artery with the lower edge about 2 cm above the elbow crease, and names cuff fitting as one of the leading sources of measurement error (AHA 2019 statement). The physical difficulty is wrapping a floppy 50 cm band round a limb with two hands, in the right order, snug and in place.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases (x forward, y to the robot's left); heights above the table top. Arm board: grey foam, 56 x 12 x 3 cm, centred at (30.0, 6.0). Training arm: life-size vinyl arm, palm up on the board along x, hand towards the robot (wrist at x 9), elbow at x 30, shoulder end at x 56; upper arm 10 cm across (31.4 cm round), its underside 4 mm above the board; elbow crease marked across the top of the arm at x 31.5; the brachial artery marked with a red line along the near (robot's right) side of the upper arm, level with its axis. Cuff: adult reusable blood-pressure cuff, 50 cm long and 16 cm wide, 0.10 kg, nylon over a 16 x 30 cm bladder (the AHA adult size for 27-34 cm arms) in its first 30 cm; a white index line across it 16 cm from the bladder end; a 10 cm hook (Velcro) tab on the inner face of the other end; loop fabric on the whole outer face; a 16 x 16 mm stiffened foam hem across each end. It lies open and flat across the board under the upper arm, along y, its lower edge 2.5 cm above the crease (x 34.0 to 50.0), the bladder end towards the robot's right (its end at y -18), the hook end to the left (its end at y 32); the parts beyond the board's edges lie on the table.
scoring: Tools: a ruler, a phone photo from above and from the side, a 6 mm dowel. Scored on the final state, after both grippers are clear. 0 unless the cuff goes once round the arm. 0.25: wrapped. 0.5: also fastened (the hook tab pressed flat onto the cuff's outer face and still holding the cuff closed at the end). 0.75: also in place: lower edge 1.5 to 3.5 cm above the crease, the lower edge's distance from the crease differing by under 2 cm round the arm (not spiralled), and the index line within 2 cm of the artery mark. 1.0: also snug: the 6 mm dowel cannot be pushed under the cuff's edge at the top or either side of the arm. In simulation the same rules are computed from the plates' poses: fastened = at least 3 hook plates lying within 2 mm of the plate under them for 0.5 s; snug = mean gap of the inner layer to the skin at most 6 mm.
reset_notes: Open the cuff (peel the hook tab off), lay it flat across the board under the upper arm with its lower edge on the 2.5 cm mark and the bladder end to the robot's right, the ends on the table. Nothing is consumed; the cuff's hook-and-loop is good for thousands of closures.
fidelity: The arm and board are fixed (the upper arm collides as a 10 cm capsule with skin-like friction; the visible arm is a mesh 1 mm proud of it). The cuff is 20 rigid 2.5 cm plates hinged across its width with light bending springs; it cannot stretch or crumple. The hook-and-loop is a rule: fastened when 3 hook plates are pressed flat onto the cuff for 0.5 s; nothing holds them after that but friction and gravity.
